nameStory: Risso's dolphin is named after Giovanni Antonio Risso, an Italian naturalist who first described this species in the early 1800s. The scientific name 'Grampus' comes from an old French word meaning 'big fish,' though dolphins are actually mammals, not fish!
description: Risso's dolphins are robust, medium-sized marine mammals that grow to about 10 feet long. They have a distinctive bulbous head and lack the prominent beak that many other dolphins have. What makes them truly remarkable is their heavily scarred skin that appears bright white against their darker gray base color, creating a unique patchwork appearance that makes each individual recognizable.

idTips.label: Scarring Pattern
idTips.description: Covered in distinctive white scars that create a mottled, scratched appearance across their dark gray skin - these scars feel smooth and slightly raised when touched and are caused by interactions with other dolphins and squid

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: About 10 feet long with a stocky, robust build and a distinctive bulbous forehead that feels firm and rounded, lacking the elongated beak of most dolphins

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Travel in tight social groups of 10-50 individuals, often seen surfacing together in synchronized movements and diving to great depths for extended periods

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deep waters along continental shelf edges where they can access their preferred squid prey at depths up to 2,000 feet

habitat: In New England waters, Risso's dolphins are found in deeper offshore areas along the continental shelf edge, typically in cold to temperate waters. They prefer areas where the seafloor drops off steeply, giving them access to the deep-water squid and cephalopods that make up their diet.

seasonality.spring: May be spotted in New England waters as they follow squid populations, though sightings remain very rare in our region.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time for potential sightings in deeper offshore waters, when warmer surface temperatures make boat trips to their deep-water habitat more feasible.
seasonality.fall: Possible sightings continue as dolphins follow prey movements, though their unpredictable nature makes encounters challenging to predict.
seasonality.winter: Rarely observed due to harsh offshore conditions, though they may still be present in deeper waters beyond typical observation range.

funFact: Risso's dolphins are living artwork - each individual's unique pattern of white scars tells the story of their life, created by playful interactions with other dolphins and battles with giant squid in the deep ocean darkness!
confusionNotes: Could potentially be confused with pilot whales, but Risso's dolphins are smaller, lack the pilot whale's pronounced melon forehead, and have that distinctive white scarring pattern that pilot whales don't possess.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Grampus' (meaning 'big fish'), these are mammals that breathe air and nurse their young - the old naming reflects how little early naturalists understood about marine mammal biology.
compareHints: Risso's dolphin is the only species in its genus Grampus, making it unique among dolphins. Its closest relatives are actually the larger pilot whales and false killer whales, but Risso's dolphins are distinguished by their smaller size, bulbous head without an extended beak, and especially their characteristic white scarring that the others lack.
